 Hand Sanitizer Recall: Why They Happen and How to Check 
 Guide Patient Safety & Infection Prevention Hand Sanitizer Recall: Why They Happen and How to Check
 Why hand sanitizers are recalled or listed by FDA, and how to check a product by manufacturer, distributor and NDC instead of brand name.
 Written and maintained by CASRAI Editorial Board 
 Last updated 1 November 2026 
 X 
 LinkedIn 
 Facebook 
 Copy link 
 General product-safety information, not medical advice. 
 Short answer
 A hand sanitizer recall is a company’s voluntary step to pull a defective product or warn about a risk. It is a different thing from the FDA’s “hand sanitizers consumers should not use” table. To check a product, match its manufacturer, distributor and NDC against FDA records rather than relying on the brand name, because one brand can be made by several manufacturers.
 Definition and scope
 FDA describes a drug recall as a company’s voluntary step to pull a defective drug from the market or to warn of a risk, and calls it one of the most effective ways to protect consumers from a defective or potentially harmful medicine (FDA Drug Recalls page, content current 26 October 2026).
 FDA also published a separate, searchable table titled “FDA updates on hand sanitizers consumers should not use”. It lists products by manufacturer, product, NDC, distributor, product status and the date each was added. That table is a warning list. A listing there is not the same event as a company recall.
 Why products are recalled or listed
 The reasons recorded in FDA’s table are more varied than the 2020 news coverage suggested. Three reasons appear in the table:
 Methanol, reported by the manufacturer. Entries such as “Product contains methanol based on information provided by the manufacturer”.
 Contaminants found by FDA testing. Entries such as “FDA tested product; contains unacceptable level of acetal and acetaldehyde contaminants”.
 No records provided. Many entries state that the manufacturer “did not respond to multiple FDA requests for records related to drug manufacturing and product quality”.
 So a listing does not always mean a laboratory result for that exact bottle. Some entries rest on a manufacturer’s own information, and some on a manufacturer’s silence.
 The methanol concern became a public-health alert in 2020. In CDC Health Alert Network advisory 00434 (distributed 5 July 2020, archived), CDC reported that some hand sanitizers made in Mexico had been found to contain a significant amount of methanol, while most commercial products contain ethanol or isopropanol. It described seven patients in New Mexico with serious adverse events, all with significant blood methanol concentrations, four of whom died, and six further patients in Arizona, one with permanent blindness.
 How to check a product
 A checklist based on the FDA pages and the CDC advisory:
 Find the manufacturer, distributor and NDC on the label. FDA advises identifying a product this way, and its table can be searched by product or brand, manufacturer, distributor and NDC. The label guide at hand sanitizer label shows where these appear.
 Search the manufacturer and the NDC, not only the brand. A distributor’s brand may use multiple manufacturers, so a warning about one manufacturer may not cover every product sold under that brand.
 Check the FDA drug recalls table as well. It is filterable by company and can be downloaded as a spreadsheet.
 Read the recall status. FDA states that recalls not indicated as terminated are either ongoing or completed.
 FDA do-not-use list versus the recalls database

 Where newer recalls are announced 
 The practical consequence for clinic and procurement staff is that the do-not-use table is a historical reference. A product’s absence from it says nothing about events after April 2024, so the recalls database is the place to look for newer ones.
 Where it matters for labs, clinics and supply decisions
 Staff who stock or issue sanitizer can use the checklist above to keep a short record per product: manufacturer, distributor, NDC and the date it was checked against each FDA source. Related guides: hand sanitizer disposal and isopropyl alcohol disposal for disposal in general, hand sanitizer ingredients and how to use hand sanitizer for general product information, and hand sanitizer expiration , since expiry is a separate matter.
 For the wider topic area, see the patient safety hub.
 Common misunderstandings
 “Every listed product was tested and found toxic.”
 Not necessarily. Entries cite manufacturer-reported methanol, FDA testing results, or a manufacturer’s failure to supply records, as described above.
 “A brand name is enough to know whether a product is affected.”
 FDA notes that a distributor brand may use multiple manufacturers. Check the manufacturer and NDC.
 “The do-not-use list is the current list.”
 The page states that it is no longer being updated. Newer recalls are on the FDA drug recalls page and database.
 “Sanitizer contamination only matters if the product is swallowed.”
 The CDC advisory covers ingestion cases, which is why the 2020 alert was issued.
 FAQ
 How do I know if my hand sanitizer has been recalled?
 Look up its manufacturer, distributor and NDC on the FDA drug recalls page and, for products from 2023 to April 2024, in FDA’s do-not-use table.
 Why were hand sanitizers recalled?
 FDA’s table records methanol reported by the manufacturer, unacceptable levels of acetal and acetaldehyde found in FDA testing, and manufacturers that did not provide records on drug manufacturing and quality.
 What does it mean if a product is on the list?
 It means FDA flagged that manufacturer’s product for one of the reasons in the table, such as manufacturer-reported methanol, contaminants found in FDA testing, or missing records. It is a warning entry, and it is not a company recall by itself.
 Is the FDA hand sanitizer list still updated?
 No. The page says it is no longer being updated and points to the drug recalls page and recalls database.
